blocks.text: Diffraction of waves is the bending of waves around the sharp edges or corners of obstacles or the spreading of waves beyond a barrier. It occurs when a wave encounters a physical barrier or an opening (a slit) that is comparable in size to the wavelength of the wave. The longer the wavelength, the greater the spreading and vice versa.

blocks.alt: Two diagrams with the same gap in a barrier. Left: closely spaced straight wavefronts (small wavelength) pass the gap and spread only a little: Small wavelength, Small diffraction. Right: widely spaced wavefronts (large wavelength) spread out in wide half circles: Large wavelength, Large diffraction.
blocks.caption: Diffraction through a slit (PDF page 157): small wavelength, small diffraction; large wavelength, large diffraction (original drawing after the textbook's picture in this box).

blocks.text: Diffraction can be observed in various types of waves, including water waves, sound waves, light waves and electromagnetic waves.
Some examples of the phenomenon of diffraction include:

items: Hearing of sound waves around corners or through door way from where they were generated as sound waves bend around the corners.
Diffraction of X-rays by crystals as the spacing between the regular arrays of atoms is of the order of X-rays wavelength.

blocks.text: Diffraction is a fundamental aspect of wave behaviour and has many practical applications in various fields.
